prompts.title: Business Requirements Document Drafter
prompts.description: Turns project notes into a structured business requirements document with scope, requirements and open questions.
prompts.full_prompt:
Act as a senior business analyst experienced in writing business requirements documents for enterprise projects.

Context:
I am documenting the business needs for [PROJECT NAME]. Stakeholders have shared informal notes and emails, and the delivery team needs a single agreed document before design starts.

Task:
Draft a business requirements document from the input. Separate business objectives, in-scope and out-of-scope items, functional requirements, non-functional requirements, assumptions, dependencies and risks. Give every requirement a unique ID and a priority (Must, Should, Could).

Input:
Stakeholder notes and background: [SOURCE TEXT]. Known constraints or deadlines: [DEADLINE].

Output format:
A document with numbered sections: 1 Purpose, 2 Objectives, 3 Scope, 4 Requirements (table: ID, requirement, rationale, priority), 5 Assumptions and dependencies, 6 Risks, 7 Open questions.

Constraints:
- Use only information from the input; mark anything inferred as 'Assumption'.
- Write each requirement as one testable statement starting with 'The system shall' or 'The business shall'.
- Keep the whole document under 1,200 words.
- Do not include personal data.

Quality criteria:
- Each requirement is unambiguous, testable and not duplicated.
- Open questions list every gap you found in the input.
- State your assumptions explicitly and briefly explain the rationale for each priority.
prompts.use_case: Drafting a BRD from raw notes
prompts.expected_output: A structured BRD with prioritised requirement table and a list of open questions.

example_inputs.SOURCE TEXT: Procurement wants suppliers to upload invoices online; finance needs automatic matching to POs; IT limits downtime to 2 hours.

prompts.example_output: Eight numbered sections, about 25 requirements with IDs such as BR-001, and 6 to 10 open questions for stakeholders.
prompts.why_it_works: It forces a standard BRD structure, separates facts from assumptions and demands testable, uniquely numbered requirements, which reduces rework later.
customization_tips: Add the names of approvers to the Open questions section.
Ask for a traceability column if your organisation uses requirement tracing.
Paste the template headings your company uses into the Output format.
common_mistakes: Pasting only a title and expecting detail.
Not stating the scope boundary, which leads to vague requirements.
Accepting the draft without confirming assumptions with stakeholders.

prompts.title: Process-Mapping Assistant
prompts.description: Converts a verbal process description into numbered steps, swimlanes, decision points and pain points.
prompts.full_prompt:
Act as a business process analyst skilled in as-is process documentation and BPMN-style thinking.

Context:
I am mapping the current process for [PROCESS NAME] in my team. People describe it differently, so I need one clear, shared version before we look for improvements.

Task:
Convert the description into a structured process map. Identify actors, steps, decision points, handoffs, systems used and delays. Then list the top pain points and quick-win improvements.

Input:
Process description from interviews or notes: [SOURCE TEXT]

Output format:
First a numbered step list with the actor for each step. Then a table (Step, Actor, System, Decision or handoff, Pain point). Finish with a Mermaid flowchart code block.

Constraints:
- Do not invent steps; list unclear parts under 'Questions to confirm'.
- Use verbs for step names (for example 'Review invoice').
- Limit improvements to five, ranked by effort versus impact.

Quality criteria:
- Every decision point has all its outcomes described.
- Handoffs between teams are visible.
- Each improvement links to a specific pain point.
prompts.expected_output: A numbered process, a pain-point table and a flowchart definition.

example_inputs.SOURCE TEXT: Paste the notes or document here

prompts.example_output: A 12-step process with three decision points, a table of pain points, and a Mermaid flowchart.
prompts.why_it_works: Asking for actors, systems and handoffs makes hidden delays visible, and the Mermaid block gives a diagram you can paste into documentation tools.
customization_tips: Add 'Include SLA times for each step' if you measure turnaround.
Request swimlanes per department instead of per actor.
Ask for a future-state version in a second pass.
common_mistakes: Describing the ideal process instead of the real one.
Leaving out exceptions and rework loops.
Skipping the confirmation of unclear steps.
constraints: Do not invent steps; list unclear parts under 'Questions to confirm'.
Use verbs for step names (for example 'Review invoice').
Limit improvements to five, ranked by effort versus impact.

prompts.title: Root-Cause Analysis with 5 Whys and Fishbone
prompts.description: Guides a structured root-cause investigation and separates symptoms, causes and corrective actions.
prompts.full_prompt:
Act as a continuous-improvement analyst trained in root-cause analysis methods.

Context:
We keep experiencing the following recurring problem: [PROBLEM DESCRIPTION]. Previous fixes did not last, so I need to find the underlying cause rather than treating symptoms.

Task:
Perform a root-cause analysis. Define the problem precisely, run a 5 Whys chain, group possible causes in fishbone categories (People, Process, Technology, Data, Environment), pick the most likely root causes and propose corrective and preventive actions.

Input:
Facts, metrics and timeline: [DATA]. Actions already tried: [PREVIOUS ACTIONS].

Output format:
Sections: Problem statement, 5 Whys table, Fishbone table by category, Most likely root causes with evidence needed, Corrective actions, Preventive actions, Metrics to confirm the fix worked.

Constraints:
- Label each cause as 'Confirmed by the input' or 'Hypothesis to verify'.
- Do not stop at human error; ask why the process allowed it.
- Maximum one page of text.

Quality criteria:
- The 5 Whys chain is logically connected, each answer explaining the previous one.
- Actions are specific, with a suggested owner role.
- State assumptions and what data would confirm each hypothesis.
prompts.expected_output: A problem statement, linked 5 Whys chain, fishbone grouping and action plan.

example_inputs.PROBLEM DESCRIPTION: About 8% of invoices are paid late every month
example_inputs.DATA: Paste the table, export or figures here

prompts.example_output: A 5 Whys chain ending in a process-design cause, a 5-category fishbone, and 6 corrective and preventive actions.
prompts.why_it_works: Labelling causes as confirmed or hypothetical prevents the AI from presenting guesses as facts, and the prevent step keeps the fix lasting.
customization_tips: Add the cost of the problem to prioritise causes.
Ask for a 'who should verify' column.
Run the analysis again after you collect missing data.
common_mistakes: Describing a symptom as the problem statement.
Accepting the first 'why' as the root cause.
constraints: Label each cause as 'Confirmed by the input' or 'Hypothesis to verify'.
Do not stop at human error; ask why the process allowed it.
Maximum one page of text.

prompts.title: Change-Impact Analysis
prompts.description: Assesses how a proposed change affects people, processes, systems, data and customers.
prompts.full_prompt:
Act as a change-management analyst who assesses organisational impact.

Context:
We plan to introduce [CHANGE DESCRIPTION] by [DEADLINE]. Leaders want to understand who and what will be affected before approving the rollout.

Task:
Perform a change-impact analysis across People, Process, Technology, Data, Customers and Compliance. Rate each impact High, Medium or Low, explain why, and recommend mitigation and communication actions.

Input:
Details of the change and current state: [SOURCE TEXT].

Output format:
A table (Area, Impacted group, Impact description, Rating, Mitigation, Owner role) followed by a short summary of the three highest impacts and a readiness checklist.

Constraints:
- Base ratings only on the input; list questions where information is missing.
- Keep the summary below 120 words.
- Do not suggest actions that need a budget above what is stated.

Quality criteria:
- Every rating has a one-sentence justification.
- Mitigations are practical and time-bound.
- Missing information is listed as questions.
prompts.expected_output: An impact table, summary of top impacts and readiness checklist.

example_inputs.CHANGE DESCRIPTION: Moving order entry from email to a self-service portal
example_inputs.SOURCE TEXT: Paste the notes or document here

prompts.example_output: A table with about 12 rows across six areas, three top impacts and a ten-item readiness checklist.
prompts.why_it_works: The fixed impact areas stop important groups such as compliance or customers from being forgotten, and ratings with reasons make the output reviewable.
customization_tips: Add specific departments to the impacted groups.
Request a RACI for mitigation actions.
Add a second table for training needs.
common_mistakes: Ignoring the readiness of the people affected.
constraints: Base ratings only on the input; list questions where information is missing.
Keep the summary below 120 words.
Do not suggest actions that need a budget above what is stated.

prompts.title: Stakeholder Analysis and Engagement Plan
prompts.description: Maps stakeholders by influence and interest and proposes an engagement approach for each.
prompts.full_prompt:
Act as an experienced business analyst and stakeholder-engagement coach.

Context:
I am starting [PROJECT NAME] and need to understand who matters, what they care about and how to keep them engaged.

Task:
Analyse the stakeholder list. For each stakeholder assess influence and interest (High, Medium, Low), main concern, likely attitude and the best engagement approach. Group them into a power-interest grid.

Input:
Stakeholder list with roles: [DATA].

Output format:
A table (Stakeholder, Role, Influence, Interest, Main concern, Attitude, Engagement approach, Frequency) and a four-quadrant summary: Manage closely, Keep satisfied, Keep informed, Monitor.

Constraints:
- Mark attitude as 'Assumed' when the input gives no evidence.
- Suggest at most one engagement approach per stakeholder.
- Neutral, respectful language about individuals.

Quality criteria:
- No stakeholder in the input is omitted.
- Engagement approaches differ according to the quadrant.
- Assumptions are clearly flagged.
prompts.expected_output: A stakeholder table plus a power-interest quadrant summary.

example_inputs.DATA: Sponsor (CFO), Product owner, IT security lead, Customer support manager, External vendor PM

prompts.example_output: A table of 10 stakeholders with engagement approaches and a quadrant list.
prompts.why_it_works: Requiring an 'Assumed' label on attitude keeps speculation visible, and quadrants turn a long list into actions.
customization_tips: Add a 'Success looks like' column for each stakeholder.
Include external stakeholders such as vendors.
common_mistakes: Writing opinions about named people as facts.
Forgetting hidden stakeholders such as support teams.

prompts.title: Current-State to Future-State Gap Analysis
prompts.description: Compares current and target capabilities and turns gaps into prioritised recommendations.
prompts.full_prompt:
Act as a business architect who performs capability and gap analysis.

Context:
Our team currently works as described in the current state, and leadership wants to reach the future state for [TOPIC]. I need to see the gaps and decide what to fix first.

Task:
Compare the current and future state across Process, People, Technology and Data. Identify each gap, its business impact, effort to close it (Low, Medium, High) and a recommended action. Then prioritise using impact versus effort.

Input:
Current state: [CURRENT STATE]. Future state: [FUTURE STATE].

Output format:
A table (Dimension, Current, Target, Gap, Impact, Effort, Recommended action, Priority) and a short roadmap grouped into Now, Next and Later.

Constraints:
- Do not add capabilities that are not in the target state.
- Limit the roadmap to nine items.
- Use plain business language, no jargon.

Quality criteria:
- Each gap is traceable to both input descriptions.
- Priorities follow a stated rule such as high impact with low effort first.
- Assumptions are listed.
prompts.expected_output: A gap table with a prioritised Now/Next/Later roadmap.

example_inputs.TOPIC: Migration of the customer database to a new CRM
example_inputs.CURRENT STATE: Manual order entry, three spreadsheets, weekly reporting
example_inputs.FUTURE STATE: Automated order intake, single data source, daily dashboards

prompts.example_output: A table of 12 gaps and a three-column roadmap.
prompts.why_it_works: Comparing both states dimension by dimension exposes gaps systematically, while the priority rule makes the roadmap explainable.
customization_tips: Add a cost estimate column if you have budgets.
Add dimensions such as Governance or Compliance.
common_mistakes: Writing the future state as slogans rather than capabilities.
Mixing solutions into the gap description.
constraints: Do not add capabilities that are not in the target state.
Limit the roadmap to nine items.
Use plain business language, no jargon.

prompts.title: Executive Decision Brief
prompts.description: Creates a one-page brief that frames a decision, compares options and recommends a course of action.
prompts.full_prompt:
Act as a strategy advisor who writes decision briefs for senior executives.

Context:
A decision about [DECISION TOPIC] must be made by [DEADLINE]. The audience is time-poor executives who need clarity on options, risks and a recommendation.

Task:
Write a decision brief that states the decision required, background, options (including do nothing), evaluation against criteria, risks, recommendation and next steps.

Input:
Facts, figures and constraints: [DATA]. Evaluation criteria: [CRITERIA].

Output format:
A one-page brief with headings: Decision required, Why now, Options, Comparison table (options by criteria), Recommendation, Risks and mitigations, Next steps with owners.

Constraints:
- Maximum 350 words plus one table.
- Lead with the recommendation in the first two lines.
- Use only the supplied figures; flag missing ones.
- Neutral tone, no sales language.

Quality criteria:
- A reader can decide in under three minutes.
- The 'do nothing' option is evaluated fairly.
- Recommendation follows from the comparison, with a short explanation of the reasoning.
prompts.expected_output: A one-page decision brief with comparison table and next steps.

example_inputs.DECISION TOPIC: Build or buy a ticket-routing tool
example_inputs.DATA: Paste the table, export or figures here
example_inputs.CRITERIA: Cost, time to value, security, maintainability

prompts.example_output: A 350-word brief with three options, a 5-criteria table and a recommendation.
prompts.why_it_works: Starting with the recommendation and including 'do nothing' matches how executives read, and the criteria table keeps the reasoning visible.
customization_tips: Add the decision-maker's name and their known preferences.
State a budget ceiling as a constraint.
Ask for a risk heat-map table.
common_mistakes: Burying the recommendation at the end.

Lead with the recommendation in the first two lines.
Use only the supplied figures; flag missing ones.
Neutral tone, no sales language.

prompts.description: Produces a concise, honest project status report with RAG status, progress, risks and decisions needed.

Act as an experienced project manager who writes clear status reports for sponsors and steering committees.

Context:
I manage [PROJECT NAME] and must send the status report for this period. The sponsor wants to understand progress, problems and decisions without reading long updates.

Task:
Write the status report from my notes. Give an overall RAG status with a one-sentence reason, then progress against plan, achievements, planned next period work, top risks and issues, and decisions or help needed.

My raw notes for the period: [SOURCE TEXT]. Reporting period: [REPORTING PERIOD].

Headings: Overall status (RAG + reason), Achievements, Next period, Schedule and budget, Top 3 risks and issues (with owner and action), Decisions needed. Use bullets, maximum 250 words.

- The RAG status is consistent with the details below it.
- Every risk has an owner and a next action.
- A sponsor can read it in two minutes.

example_inputs.SOURCE TEXT: Testing finished for module A, module B two days late due to vendor, budget at 62% spent.

prompts.example_output: A 250-word report with Amber status, three risks with owners and two decisions.

Leaving out the decision you need.

Act as a risk-management specialist who maintains RAID logs for large projects.

Context:
I am reviewing risks for [PROJECT NAME]. The project is in the [PROJECT PHASE] phase, and I need a defendable register before the next governance meeting.

Task:
Analyse the description and create a risk and issue register. For each risk give cause, event, consequence, probability (1-5), impact (1-5), score, response strategy (Avoid, Mitigate, Transfer, Accept), action, owner role and trigger. Separate current issues from future risks.

- Maximum 12 risks.
- Mark scores as 'Initial estimate' for review by the team.

Quality criteria:
- Risks are future events; issues are current problems.
- Mitigation actions are concrete and not generic.
- State assumptions behind the scores.

prompts.example_output: A sorted register of 10 risks, 3 issues and a top-3 discussion list.

prompts.title: Project Charter Builder
prompts.description: Drafts a one-to-two page project charter with objectives, scope, deliverables, governance and success measures.
prompts.full_prompt:
Act as a PMO lead who writes project charters for approval boards.

We are initiating [PROJECT NAME] and the sponsor needs a charter to authorise the work. Not all details are known yet.
